title: Generative AI for Teachers’ Self-Directed Professional Development: A Mixed-Methods Study
extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines how K-12 teachers use generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, for self-directed professional development (SDPD). The authors ask how ChatGPT supports instructional practice, how teachers use it within their own professional learning processes, and how teachers perceive its usefulness for SDPD. The study is framed by Garrison’s self-directed learning model, focusing on self-management, self-monitoring, and motivation.

The quantitative phase surveyed 298 U.S.-based K-12 teachers who had experience using ChatGPT for teaching and professional development. The qualitative phase included five semi-structured interviews and analysis of teachers’ ChatGPT interaction logs or related documents. Participants reported using ChatGPT mainly for lesson planning, generating pedagogical ideas, creating activities or materials, and saving time in planning and organization. Interviewees included elementary and high school teachers as well as teachers working in adult/community and college/university contexts; the findings highlighted experience differences and varied subject areas, including English language arts, reading, social science, and social studies/history/government/economics.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can function as a flexible, just-in-time support tool that lowers the barrier to engaging in SDPD, especially when teachers face time pressure and limited formal PD opportunities. Teachers generally used the tool critically, revising outputs based on their expertise and classroom needs. The authors argue that generative AI may expand teachers’ informal professional learning by providing structure, ideas, and motivation, while also raising concerns about shallow engagement, uneven digital literacy, and the need for stronger institutional support and AI-specific training.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used to generate, revise, and discuss text, ideas, and feedback through natural-language prompting.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a self-directed professional development tool for K-12 teachers in the United States; teachers used it for lesson-plan inspiration, course planning, generating materials, answering questions, and reflecting on teaching practice.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods study of 298 K-12 U.S. teachers, participants reported using ChatGPT most often for inspiration for classroom pedagogies, class activities, and lesson plans (19.49%), generating practice questions/quizzes (17.97%), and creating customized educational content (15.75%). Interviewees likewise described using it to structure lesson planning and curriculum design, including an 18-week pacing guide for a high school anthropology course.
findings.measure: Self-reported educational activities/use cases with ChatGPT; interview descriptions of lesson-planning use

findings.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT supported self-management in SDPD by helping them organize activities, manage time, and apply learning strategies (e.g., organizing activities M=4.81, managing time M=4.70). Interviewees repeatedly said the tool saved planning time and reduced cognitive load, allowing them to focus on other classroom responsibilities.
findings.measure: Likert-scale self-management items and interview themes about time management/organization

findings.finding_summary: Teachers were motivated to use ChatGPT for SDPD, with strong agreement on wanting to improve teaching practice (M=3.87), learn new ideas (M=3.94), and enjoy learning through ChatGPT (M=3.96), but the paper also notes passive motivation due to teaching pressure and limited room for professional advancement. Several teachers said ChatGPT lowered the entry threshold for SDPD by making it easier to start planning and learning.
findings.measure: Motivation to use ChatGPT for SDPD; interview accounts of barriers and motivators

findings.finding_summary: Teachers generally felt responsible for and capable of directing their own learning with ChatGPT, including setting goals, seeking help, and following plans (e.g., responsibility for learning M=4.19; high learning standards M=4.04). Interviewees described iterative refinement of AI-generated lesson materials and using ChatGPT to break ideas into smaller pieces.
findings.measure: Self-monitoring and self-management Likert items; interview themes on reflection and revision

findings.finding_summary: Participants generally agreed that they critically evaluated ChatGPT's instructional ideas (M=4.17) and felt confident interacting with the tool (M=4.04), but confidence in the accuracy of its information was more variable (M=3.46). The authors interpret this as teachers using a critical mindset and relying on their own expertise to edit and humanize AI outputs.
findings.measure: Perceptions of ChatGPT's functionality and accuracy; interview reflections on critical use

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods empirical study with a moderate sample size, but it relies on self-report survey data, a very small interview sample, and descriptive analysis rather than experimental or quasi-experimental estimation. That makes it useful evidence, but not high-credibility causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceived effects on planning, motivation, self-management, and critical reflection, but it does not provide causal effect sizes or student outcome gains. Impact is therefore promising but quantitatively unclear.
